land.text: Thrace, the Chersonese and the west Pontic coast, 'the government of Thrace' assigned to Lysimachus at the Partition of Babylon in June 323

predecessors.note: A satrapy of the nominal Macedonian empire until Lysimachus 'followed the example of Antigonus and assumed the title of king' in 306/305; the macedonian-empire dossier tints Thrace as its vassal 323-306 (rule 4).

land.text: Lysimachus's Asia Minor, 'Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor', taken by Seleucus after Corupedium (February 281): 'Seleucids gain control of Anatolia'

successors.note: Pergamon's Philetaerus went over to Seleucus; Cliopatria's Pergamon row starts in 279 (kingdom-of-pergamon, group me-05).

land.text: Macedon and Thrace, seized by Ptolemy Keraunos in September 281 ('acclaimed king by the army at Lysimachia'), ruled by Keraunos, Meleager, Antipater Etesias and Sosthenes through the Gallic invasion, and finally won by Antigonus II Gonatas in 277

successors.note: Cliopatria draws nobody in Macedon and Thrace between the end of this row (282) and 'Antigonid Macedonia' (277): the 281-277 interregnum of Ptolemy Keraunos and Sosthenes is a gap flagged in the notes (suggested slug macedon-interregnum-281). Under rule 8 the land may be left as nobody's land until 277, with Thrace north of the Haemus becoming Celtic (Tyle, 277) and the interior Thracian again.

capitals.name: Lysimachia (Chersonese)
capitals.note: 'The city was built by Lysimachus in 309 BC, when he was preparing for war with his rivals'; 'Lysimachus no doubt made Lysimachia the capital of his kingdom'. Infobox location Kavakköy/Bolayır, Gelibolu (40.583 N, 26.883 E). Where Lysimachus sat in 323-309 the pages do not say; the Chersonese (Cardia) is the natural guess but is not sourced, so no capital is drawn before 309.

rulers.name: Lysimachus
rulers.note: Satrap/strategos of Thrace 323; king 306/305 ('Thrace 306-281, Asia Minor 301-281, Macedon 288-281' in the infobox); killed at Corupedium, 281. Co-regents: Agathocles (son, executed 284/283) is not counted.

minus.text: the Odrysian interior of Seuthes III around Seuthopolis (near Kazanlak)

correction.text: Thrace as Cliopatria draws it (coast, Chersonese, Pontic cities, Haemus to the Danube), less the Odrysian interior that Seuthes III kept

keyframe_review.note: 151 k km2, Danube to the Chersonese. The whole of Thrace to the Danube is too much for 323: Seuthes III 'continued in opposition to the new governor Lysimachus', in 322 the two 'fought each other to a draw and each withdrew from battle', and he 'ruled only part of Thrace and shared space with both the Macedonian Lysimachus' and other Thracian rulers; 'Perhaps around 320 BC, Seuthes III established his residence at' Seuthopolis near Kazanlak. Cliopatria's Odrysian row ends in 338, so that interior has no other owner: the ledger carries it as a contest in 322 and again 313-310 (rule 6 blend; fix run, it was 323-310 on the strength of an undated sentence), after which Seuthes 'settled for peace with Lysimachus' and 'kept his autonomy' (a vassal tint, rule 4, until Seuthes disappears from the record). The whole shape is also the empire's vassal tint until 306 (rule 4).

minus.text: the Odrysian interior of Seuthes III

correction.text: as the 323 shape, less the Odrysian interior

keyframe_review.note: Identical to the 323 shape (151 k km2); the same correction applies. Lysimachus sided with Cassander against Polyperchon in 319-316 without territorial change on the pages opened.

minus.text: the Odrysian interior of Seuthes III (to 310, then a vassal tint)

correction.text: Thrace less the Odrysian interior; from 310 the interior may be drawn as Lysimachus's vassal (Seuthes 'kept his autonomy')

keyframe_review.note: 151 k km2, 315-302. In 313 'Seuthes III supported the revolt of Callatis' and the west Pontic cities with Antigonus's help; Lysimachus 'finally subdued Callatis in 310 BC'. The Chersonese gains Lysimachia (309). The shape is right for the coast and the Chersonese; the extension to the Danube is Cliopatria's and not confirmed by the pages (the Getae beyond the Danube were never held: Lysimachus 'was taken prisoner by Dromichaetes' in 292 and released).

correction.text: Thrace plus the share of Antigonus's Asia Minor awarded after Ipsus: 'Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor'; not Lycia, Pamphylia or southern Caria

keyframe_review.note: 411 k km2, bbox to 35.6 E and down to 36.2 N. After Ipsus (301) Lysimachus 'received Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor'; Bithynia stays independent (Cliopatria's own row). The southern reach to 36.2 N takes in the Lycian and Pamphylian coasts, which the page does not give him (they are Ptolemaic in this period) and southern Caria, which was Rhodian/Ptolemaic: adjust by trimming the south to the Maeander line. 'In 302 BC Lysimachus married Amastris' and gained Heraclea Pontica's sphere (conf 2). The 302 invasion of Asia Minor is a contest with the Antigonid kingdom (rule 6).

correction.text: the 301 shape for 291-289 only: Thrace plus Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia, Mysia, the Troad and the Heraclea-Amastris coast, without Macedon: Central Macedonia is Demetrius's until he is driven out (288 on the Pyrrhus page and the Lysimachus infobox, 287 in the Lysimachus text)

keyframe_review.note: 411 k km2 for the Cliopatria shape of 291-285, which here holds only for 291-289: it carries no Macedon, and from 288 Central Macedonia is Lysimachus's (new keyframe -288), so the shape of 291-289 is the 301 union of named regions and the southern Anatolian coast stays trimmed as in keyframe 3. Between 291 and 289 Central Macedonia is Demetrius's (antigonid-dynasty_-291, 127,922 km2 to 24.26 E) and must not be drawn twice. 'In 287 BC, Lysimachus and Pyrrhus in turn invaded Macedonia and drove Demetrius out' (Lysimachus page; the Pyrrhus page says 288, the Lysimachus infobox 'Macedon 288-281'). 292: the Getic captivity north of the Danube, no change of land.

The Lycian and Pamphylian coasts (Cliopatria's reach to 36.2 N) are subtracted as in the 301 keyframe's note; southern Caria is not trimmed because no page opened places it either way (the Lysimachus page names none of Caria, Lycia or Pamphylia).

keyframe_review.note: 489 k km2, to 19.3 E: the peak kingdom (Lysimachus's own row says 'Macedon 288-281'). Correct extent for 285-281; its end should be February 281, when 'Lysimachus died during the fighting' near Sardis and 'Seleucids gain control of Anatolia', not 282. Adjust, not ok: the Lycian and Pamphylian coasts that the shape reaches (36.2 N) are subtracted, since the page gives Lysimachus only Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast; southern Caria is left because no page opened places it.

region.text: Thrace, the Chersonese and the west Pontic coast

ledger.note: June 323: the Partition of Babylon. 'It was held at Babylon in June 323 BC'; 'Thrace: Lysimachus'. The Lysimachus page: he 'was appointed to the government of Thrace', 'probably with the title of strategos'. Starts as a satrapy of the nominal Macedonian empire, hence the vassal pairing that follows.

region.text: all of Lysimachus's Thrace

ledger.note: June 323 to 306/305: Lysimachus governs in the name of the kings Philip III and Alexander IV (rule 4 tint under the macedonian-empire dossier, which carries the matching pair).

region.text: the Odrysian interior of Thrace (Seuthopolis, near Kazanlak)

ledger.note: 322: Seuthes III meets Lysimachus. Seuthes was 'mustering a force of some 8,000 cavalry and 20,000 infantry in 322 BC' and 'They fought each other to a draw and each withdrew from battle' (Seuthes III page; the battle itself is undated, so read as 322). The page dates nothing earlier: that he 'continued in opposition to the new governor Lysimachus' after 323 is undated, so the contest is the 322 campaign only (fix run: it was 323-310). Cliopatria's Odrysian row ends in 338, so the counterpart is that slug used as a people.

region.text: the Odrysian interior of Thrace (Seuthopolis, near Kazanlak)

ledger.note: 322: the drawn battle ends the fighting; Seuthes keeps the interior around Seuthopolis (founded 'perhaps around 320 BC'). The Seuthes III page does not say how Seuthes stood towards Lysimachus until 313: 'Ultimately, Seuthes appears to have acknowledged the overarching authority of Lysimachus' is undated.

region.text: Callatis (Mangalia) and the west Pontic Greek cities

ledger.counterpart: Callatis and the west Pontic cities (backed by Antigonus I and Seuthes III)
ledger.note: 313: 'Seuthes III supported the revolt of Callatis' against Lysimachus 'by allying with other towns and tribes and blocking the passes of Mount Haemus'; 'Lysimachus, who then had to abandon the siege of Callatis when Antigonus I's commander Pausanias came to its aid'.

region.text: the Odrysian interior of Thrace (Seuthopolis, near Kazanlak)

ledger.note: 313: Seuthes joins the revolt of Callatis. 'In 313 BC, Seuthes III supported the revolt of Callatis' against Lysimachus, with Antigonus's backing; the interior is in contest again until the peace of 310 (next events). odrysian-kingdom has the same 313 contest and ends it in 312; the Seuthes III page dates only 'Lysimachus, who finally subdued Callatis in 310 BC', which is where this dossier ends it.

region.text: Callatis and the west Pontic cities

ledger.counterpart: Callatis and the west Pontic cities (backed by Antigonus I and Seuthes III)
ledger.note: 310: Lysimachus 'finally subdued Callatis in 310 BC'. The cities return to his rule.

region.text: the Odrysian interior

ledger.note: 310: Seuthes 'settled for peace with Lysimachus'. He 'kept his autonomy and then disappears from the narrative sources'.

region.text: the autonomous Odrysian interior under Seuthes III

ledger.note: 310 to the end of the kingdom: the Odrysian interior as an autonomous dependency (rule 4 tint). Confidence 1: the page says only that Seuthes kept his autonomy after the peace and that an inscription of the 290s or 280s is the last evidence; the subordinate relation is an inference and the Seuthopolis area may equally be drawn as nobody's land (rule 8). No vassal_end: the relation lasts to the state's end.

309: Lysimachia founded on the Chersonese (40.583 N, 26.883 E, near Bolayır/Kavakköy, Gelibolu): 'The city was built by Lysimachus in 309 BC, when he was preparing for war with his rivals'; 'Lysimachus no doubt made Lysimachia the capital of his kingdom'. No earlier capital is drawn.

region.text: Thrace

ledger.note: 306/305: 'In 306/305 BC, Lysimachus followed the example of Antigonus and assumed the title of king.' The satrapy becomes a kingdom in its own colour.
306/305: from 'Satrapy of Thrace' to 'Kingdom of Lysimachus' as Lysimachus takes the royal title (Diadochi page: the 'year of the kings', 306-304).

region.text: Hellespontine Phrygia, Lydia, Ionia and Phrygia, invaded from the Hellespont

ledger.note: 302: 'Lysimachus, reinforced by troops from Cassander, crossed over the Hellespont in 302 BC' and campaigned in Asia Minor against Antigonus; the counter-dossier (antigonid-dynasty) carries the matching pair. Rule 6 blend over western Asia Minor for 302-301.

region.text: Heraclea Pontica and Amastris on the Black Sea coast

ledger.note: c. 302: 'In 302 BC Lysimachus married Amastris', widow of the tyrant of Heraclea Pontica, which brought the city and her foundation Amastris into his sphere. Counterpart is the generic Greek-city-state slug (Heraclea was an independent polis); confidence 2 because the page states the marriage, not an annexation.

region.text: western and northern Asia Minor

ledger.note: 301: Ipsus. Antigonus 'was killed in the battle' and his kingdom 'carved up between the victors'.

region.text: 'Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor'

ledger.note: 301: the settlement after Ipsus. Lysimachus 'received Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor'; Seleucus took the lands east of them and Syria (seleucid-empire, me-05). Lycia, Pamphylia and southern Caria are not his on the pages opened: Cliopatria's shape reaches too far south.

region.text: the eastern half of Macedon (east of the Axios, approximated as Central Macedonia) and the Strymon-Nestos lands of Philippi and Amphipolis (Eastern Macedonia and Thrace), the same region antigonid-dynasty loses

ledger.note: 288 (the Lysimachus page says 287; its infobox and the Pyrrhus page 288): 'Lysimachus and Pyrrhus took advantage of Demetrius' unpopularity in Macedonia and drove Demetrius out' of his kingdom; Macedon was divided between the two. Demetrius's Macedon passes out of the antigonid-dynasty dossier (which keeps Demetrias and the Greek garrisons). The partition line is not on the pages; Central Macedonia for Lysimachus and Western Macedonia for Pyrrhus is an approximation (confidence 2). Fix run: Eastern Macedonia and Thrace added so that this gain mirrors the Antigonid 288 loss (most of it already lay in Cliopatria's Thracian shape).

region.text: Macedon, divided between Lysimachus and Pyrrhus

ledger.note: 288-285: the shared kingdom. Pyrrhus 'was king of Macedon' jointly 'with Lysimachus' from 288 (Pyrrhus infobox 'King of Macedon 288-284 BC'); the two kings held halves, uneasily (rule 6 blend over the whole of Macedon, or the two halves in the two colours, at the compiler's discretion).

region.text: Macedon

ledger.note: 285 (Lysimachus page; Pyrrhus page 284): 'In 285 BC, Lysimachus expelled Pyrrhus from Macedonia'. Pyrrhus keeps Epirus and his Greek acquisitions (Corcyra, Ambracia, Acarnania).

region.text: Pyrrhus's western share of Macedon (Upper Macedonia, approximated by Western Macedonia)

ledger.note: 285: Lysimachus sole king of Macedon. 'For a short while, the two ruled jointly but, in 285 BC, Lysimachus expelled Pyrrhus, seizing complete control for himself' (Lysimachus page; the Pyrrhus page has 284: 'In 284 BC, he was driven out of Macedon by Lysimachus'). Pyrrhus's share is approximated by Western Macedonia, as in kingdom-of-epirus and antigonid-dynasty. Thessaly is the next event.

region.text: Paeonia, which 'roughly corresponded to present-day North Macedonia' and 'also included parts of northern Greece and western Bulgaria'

ledger.note: 285/4: Lysimachus takes control of Paeonia. 'In 285/4 BC, Lysimachus took control of Paeonia, and Ariston, the son of Audoleon, escaped to Dardania.' The page does not say whether the kingdom was annexed or kept as a dependency, so it is entered as an occupation (hatched), as the kingdom-of-paeonia dossier enters it.

region.text: Thessaly apart from Demetrias and the Magnesian coast, which stayed Antigonid

ledger.note: 285: Thessaly follows Pyrrhus's Macedon. The Pyrrhus page gives Thessaly to Pyrrhus, not to Lysimachus: Antigonus Gonatas 'ceded Thessaly to him in order to make peace' (undated, after 286) and 'Pyrrhus's Greek Empire was now at its zenith: he ruled an enlarged Epirus, half of Macedonia, and Thessaly'. The Lysimachus page never mentions Thessaly, but Cliopatria's 283 shape draws its northern fringe (9 grid cells) and Gonatas was later confined to Demetrias (280). Read as Pyrrhus's Thessaly passing with his Macedon; confidence 1. One chain across the three dossiers: antigonid-dynasty loses Thessaly to Pyrrhus (288, bridged), kingdom-of-epirus should record that gain and this 285 loss.

region.text: all of Lysimachus's Asia Minor

ledger.note: February 281 (Lysimachus infobox 'Battle of Corupedium, February 281 BC'; the battle page gives no month): fought 'Near Sardis (modern-day Sart, Manisa, Turkey)', 'Seleucid victory', Lysimachus 'died during the fighting'; 'Seleucids gain control of Anatolia'.

region.text: Macedon, Thessaly and Thrace

ledger.note: 281: the European half. Seleucus 'crossed the Hellespont' to claim it and was murdered by Ptolemy Keraunos (September 281), who was 'acclaimed king by the army at Lysimachia'; 'Macedon swiftly became independent once again' (Corupedium page). The loss is dated to the battle for the map; the land is nobody's or Keraunos's until Antigonus Gonatas takes Macedon in 277 (see the identity's successor note and the notes file).

region.text: Paeonia, which 'roughly corresponded to present-day North Macedonia' and 'also included parts of northern Greece and western Bulgaria'

ledger.note: February 281: Lysimachus's hold on Paeonia ends with his death at Corupedium. The Paeonia page is silent on when his control ended; it says only that Paeonia 'was overrun and held for a time' by Brennus's Celts and that Leon 'reestablished the Paeonian kingdom' afterwards (the kingdom-of-paeonia dossier closes the occupation c. 280).

region.text: the whole kingdom

ledger.note: February 281: the kingdom ends with its king at Corupedium; it had no dynasty (Agathocles, the heir, had been executed in 284/283). Cliopatria's row ends in 282.

wars.name: Lysimachus's Thracian wars (Seuthes III and Callatis)
belligerents: Callatis and the west Pontic cities (backed by Antigonus I and Seuthes III)
wars.outcome: Drawn in 322 ('fought each other to a draw'); Callatis's revolt of 313 was broken when Lysimachus 'finally subdued Callatis in 310 BC', and Seuthes 'settled for peace' keeping his autonomy.

wars.name: Fourth War of the Diadochi (Ipsus)
wars.outcome: 'Antigonid defeat': Antigonus killed; Lysimachus 'received Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor'.
wars.note: Cassander's Macedon (macedonian-empire here) supplied the troops Lysimachus crossed with.

wars.name: Getic campaign of Lysimachus
wars.outcome: 'Lysimachus was taken prisoner by Dromichaetes' and released, 'and Lysimachus is said to have given his daughter in marriage': no land changed hands south of the Danube.
wars.note: Included so the Danube frontier of Cliopatria's shape is read as a limit, not a conquest beyond it.

wars.name: War against Demetrius in Macedon

zones.text: Macedon, 288-287; the partition and Pyrrhus's expulsion, 285

wars.outcome: Demetrius driven out and Macedon divided (288/287); Pyrrhus expelled by Lysimachus in 285 (or 284): Lysimachus sole king of Macedon.

wars.name: War of Seleucus and Lysimachus (Corupedium)
wars.outcome: 'Seleucid victory': Lysimachus killed, 'Seleucids gain control of Anatolia'; his European lands fell to Ptolemy Keraunos within the year.
wars.note: The war began after the execution of Agathocles (284/283) drove his partisans to Seleucus.

certainty.note: Thrace's interior and the Danube line are Cliopatria's; the pages give only the coast, the Chersonese and the Pontic cities as firmly held, and the Odrysian interior as disputed.
The Asian satrapies' boundaries (toward Bithynia, Seleucid Phrygia and Ptolemaic Caria-Lycia) and the 288-285 partition line in Macedon are approximate.

notes:
Cliopatria's 'Kingdom of Lysimachus' (-323..-282) is kept as one state from the satrapy of 323 (a vassal tint of the macedonian-empire dossier until the royal title of 306/305) to Corupedium, dated February 281 by the Lysimachus infobox. Three corrections matter for the map: the Thracian shapes reach the Danube although Seuthes III held the interior (contest 323-310, then an autonomous tint at confidence 1); the Asian shapes reach 36.2 N although the page gives Lysimachus only 'Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast'; and Macedon enters a year late (the 283 polygon should begin in 285, with the eastern half from 288/287 shared with Pyrrhus). Dates on which the pages disagree: Demetrius expelled 288 (Pyrrhus page, Lysimachus infobox) or 287 (Lysimachus text); Pyrrhus expelled 285 (Lysimachus) or 284 (Pyrrhus); Lysimachus king 306 or 305. The successor problem: nobody owns Macedon and Thrace between this row's end and 'Antigonid Macedonia' (277). Ptolemy Keraunos (king September 281 to January/February 279), Meleager, Antipater Etesias and Sosthenes (to 277) are not in Cliopatria; see the notes file (suggested slug macedon-interregnum-281, or an extension of antigonid-dynasty's keyframes with a rule-8 gap). Paeonia (Audoleon's kingdom): the Paeonia page, opened in the resumed run, dates Lysimachus's takeover to 285/4; it is entered as an occupation of kingdom-of-paeonia from 285 to the dossier's end (the page is silent on when his hold ended). The Agathocles affair (284/283) and Arsinoe's possession of Cassandreia, Heraclea and Ephesus are internal and not drawn.

Fix run of 2026-10-19 (after the adversarial review). Changed: (1) the Cliopatria shape of 291-285 no longer holds for the whole span: 291-289 is the 301 union of named regions, and a new keyframe -288 (288-286) adds Central Macedonia and Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, because Central Macedonia is Demetrius's until 288/287 (antigonid-dynasty draws it) and the Lysimachus page has 'In 287 BC, Lysimachus and Pyrrhus in turn invaded Macedonia'. (2) The 285-282 keyframes subtract the Lycian and Pamphylian coasts (the 283 shape reaches 36.2 N; the page gives 'Lydia, Ionia, Phrygia and the north coast of Asia Minor'); southern Caria is not named on the page either way and is left. (3) Thessaly 288-285: one chain across three dossiers: antigonid-dynasty loses it to kingdom-of-epirus (the Pyrrhus page: Gonatas 'ceded Thessaly to him'), and this dossier gains it from kingdom-of-epirus in 285 at confidence 1 (Lysimachus page silent); the 285 gain of Pyrrhus's western Macedon is its own event. kingdom-of-epirus should add the Thessaly gain and loss. (4) Seuthes III is modelled as a contest in 322 only and again 313-310, then the autonomous tint from 310 (confidence 1), following the dated sentences of the Seuthes III page (322 force and draw, 313 revolt, Callatis subdued 310). Disagreement kept: odrysian-kingdom has a contest 322-321, a vassal from 321 and a contest 313-312; the Seuthes III page says only that Seuthes 'appears to have acknowledged the overarching authority of Lysimachus', undated, and 'settled for peace' in the context of 310. (5) The 288 gain of eastern Macedon now includes Eastern Macedonia and Thrace, mirroring the Antigonid 288 loss.
